title: INTERSECT Explained
description: Learn how to use the INTERSECT operator to return distinct rows that appear in the result sets of two or more queries.

data.text: The SQL Server INTERSECT operator combines the result sets of two or more queries and returns the distinct rows that are output by both queries.

data.title: INTERSECT Syntax
data.content: Returns distinct rows that appear in both query results.

data.text: Similar to the UNION operator, the queries in the syntax above must conform to the following rules:

items: Both queries must have the same number and order of columns.
The data type of the corresponding columns must be the same or compatible.

data.text: The INTERSECT operation finds the common rows between two result sets. For example, if T1 includes 1, 2, 3 and T2 includes 2, 3, 4, the intersection returns 2 and 3.

data.title: Find Common Cities Between Customers and Stores
data.content: Return cities that appear in both customers and stores tables.
data.code:
SELECT
    city
FROM
    sales.customers
INTERSECT
SELECT
    city
FROM
    sales.stores
ORDER BY
    city;

data.text: The first query finds all cities of the customers and the second query finds the cities of the stores. The whole query, which uses INTERSECT, returns the common cities of customers and stores—i.e., the cities that are output by both queries.

data.title: INTERSECT vs INNER JOIN
data.text: INTERSECT is useful for finding common rows between two queries without needing to specify a join condition. It also removes duplicates automatically.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: INTERSECT returns distinct rows that appear in both query result sets.
It is useful for finding common elements between two data sets.
Both queries must have the same number and order of columns with compatible data types.
Add ORDER BY to the last query to sort the result set.
